questions.title: What does “information-theoretically optimal” mean for NF4 quantization in QLoRA?
questions.question_body: In the QLoRA paper, NF4 is described as an information-theoretically optimal data type for zero-mean normally distributed weights. What exact objective is being optimized here? Is it minimizing expected quantization error under a fixed codebook size, maximizing entropy usage of bins, or something like a rate–distortion bound for a source with distribution $N(0,1)$ under MSE? Can you outline the derivation or give a reference showing in what precise sense NF4 is optimal?

questions.title: How are the NF4 codebook values $q_i$ computed and why are they midpoints of quantile intervals?
questions.question_body: The paper defines $q_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(Q_X\left(\tfrac{i}{2^k+1}\right) + Q_X\left(\tfrac{i+1}{2^k+1}\right)\right)$ for a standard normal $Q_X$. Why choose midpoints between adjacent quantiles instead of the quantile boundaries themselves? Does the midpoint choice minimize expected squared error for uniform probability bins, or is there another rationale? Also, how sensitive is performance to using the exact quantiles vs approximate ones?

questions.title: Why does NF4 need an asymmetric codebook to include an exact zero, and how is bin balance preserved?
questions.question_body: The paper says symmetric $k$-bit quantization lacks an exact zero, so NF4 uses $2^{k-1}$ negative and $2^{k-1}+1$ positive levels, then removes a duplicate zero. How does this construction ensure (approximately) equal expected mass per bin for a symmetric $N(0,1)$ source? Does including the exact zero slightly skew the bin probabilities, and if so, why is that acceptable?

questions.title: Is the NF4 weight scaling step using absolute max equivalent to matching standard deviations?
questions.question_body: Step (3) of NF4 says to normalize weights into $[-1,1]$ using absolute maximum rescaling, and the text claims this is equivalent to rescaling the standard deviation to match the data type. But rescaling by absmax is not, in general, the same as matching standard deviation. Is the paper assuming the support of the normal-like weight distribution effectively fits $[-\alpha\sigma, \alpha\sigma]$, making these heuristically equivalent? Could you clarify this equivalence claim?

questions.title: How exactly is block-wise quantization applied: which dimension is blocked and how are blocks defined?
questions.question_body: For weight matrices $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times o}$, the paper uses blocksize 64 for weights and 256 for second-level scales. Are blocks contiguous in memory order after flattening, or aligned to rows/columns? If the tensor is transposed for GEMM efficiency (e.g., $W^T$ layout), does blocking follow the physical layout or the logical shape? How sensitive are results to the blocking orientation?

questions.title: How does double quantization dequantize in practice and what are the exact formats used?
questions.question_body: Double quantization stores $\mathbf{W}^{\text{k-bit}}$ with per-block $c_2$, and then quantizes $c_2$ into $c_2^{\text{FP8}}$ with per-block $c_1^{\text{FP32}}$. In the forward pass, we compute $\text{dequant}(\text{dequant}(c_1^{\text{FP32}}, c_2^{\text{k-bit}}), \mathbf{W}^{\text{k-bit}})$. Which FP8 format is used (e4m3, e5m2, or something else), and is it consistent across hardware? Are the $c_1$ blocks aligned with groups of $c_2$ blocks (size 256), and do you broadcast the recovered $c_2$ to the corresponding 64-size weight blocks?

questions.title: Where does the 0.373 bits/parameter saving from double quantization come from?
questions.question_body: The paper claims the per-parameter overhead for quantization constants drops from $32/64=0.5$ bits to $8/64 + 32/(64\cdot256)=0.127$ bits when double quantizing with 8-bit scales grouped in 256s. Could you walk through this calculation step-by-step, including the assumptions on how many weights each $c_2$ and $c_1$ serve, to reproduce the 0.127 bits/parameter figure and the 0.373 reduction?

questions.title: How does backpropagate-through-quantization work if base weights are frozen?
questions.question_body: QLoRA backpropagates gradients through the dequantized base weights to update only the LoRA adapters. The paper mentions computing derivatives like $\partial \mathbf{X}/\partial \mathbf{W}$ in BF16 while not computing $\partial E/\partial \mathbf{W}$. Could you clarify the exact computational graph? Are we simply treating the dequantized $\mathbf{W}^{\text{BF16}}$ as constants in the backward pass so gradients stop there, while the upstream Jacobians flow into $\partial E/\partial \mathbf{L}_i$?

questions.title: Would updating quantization constants during finetuning help, and how would gradients be handled?
questions.question_body: In QLoRA the base model weights and quantization constants are frozen. Hypothetically, if we wanted to finetune $c_1$ or the quantized $c_2$ (or even the NF4 codebook), how would you compute gradients through the quantization steps? Would a straight-through estimator be appropriate, and would the expected gains outweigh added instability or memory cost?

questions.title: How does QLoRA avoid runtime slowdowns despite dequantizing on every matmul?
questions.question_body: The method dequantizes 4-bit weights to BF16 whenever a layer is used, then performs matmul in BF16. Intuitively this could add overhead vs native 16-bit weights. The paper claims no runtime degradation compared to 16-bit finetuning. Are there fused CUDA kernels that combine dequantization and GEMM, or is caching used? Can you share ballpark kernel timings showing parity with 16-bit?

questions.title: What is the memory breakdown that leads to >780 GB for 16-bit finetuning of LLaMA-65B?
questions.question_body: The introduction states that regular 16-bit finetuning of LLaMA-65B requires over 780 GB of GPU memory. Can you provide a breakdown across parameters (2 bytes each), optimizer states (e.g., Adam’s $m$ and $v$, potentially 4 or 8 bytes each), gradients, activation checkpoints, and any model-parallel buffers? I’d like to reproduce the 780+ GB figure with clear assumptions about batch size and sequence length.

questions.title: Why do default LoRA settings (Q,V only) fail to match full finetuning on large models?
questions.question_body: The paper reports that applying LoRA only to the query and value projections (a common default) does not match full finetuning performance for large LLaMA bases, and that adding adapters to all linear layers is crucial. Which exact layers benefited most (e.g., attention output, MLP up/down projections)? Is there an intuition for why broader coverage matters more than increasing $r$ for a smaller subset of layers?

questions.title: LoRA rank $r$ seems less important than adapter placement—why?
questions.question_body: You note that varying the LoRA rank $r$ had little effect compared to adding adapters to more layers. From a representation capacity standpoint, why doesn’t increasing $r$ on a few layers recover performance as well as using small $r$ on many layers? Is there a theoretical or empirical explanation suggesting that coverage across the network is more impactful than rank depth in select locations?

questions.title: How are LoRA adapters scaled (the role of $s$) and initialized in QLoRA?
questions.question_body: Equation $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + s\mathbf{X}\mathbf{L}_1\mathbf{L}_2$ includes a scalar $s$. What value of $s$ do you use in practice, and how sensitive are results to this scaling? Also, how are $\mathbf{L}_1, \mathbf{L}_2$ initialized (e.g., small Gaussian, zeros except for a specific structure), and does the initialization interact with the quantized base weights in any important way?

questions.title: How do paged optimizers interact with gradient checkpointing to prevent OOM spikes?
questions.question_body: Paged optimizers rely on CUDA Unified Memory to page optimizer state between CPU and GPU when memory spikes occur (often due to long sequences with gradient checkpointing). Could you explain a typical training step’s memory timeline showing when activations, gradients, and optimizer states peak, and how paging avoids OOM? Are there scenarios where thrashing or large PCIe overhead becomes a problem?

questions.title: What are the failure modes or slowdowns of paged optimizers, and how to detect them?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that paging slowdowns are rare but not thoroughly characterized. In practice, what conditions (sequence length, microbatching, optimizer choice, number of parameters) tend to trigger noticeable paging overhead? Are there recommended telemetry signals (e.g., page fault rates) and thresholds to detect when paging begins to harm throughput?

questions.title: Why does NF4 outperform FP4 and Int4 so consistently across models and tasks?
questions.question_body: Empirically, NF4 beats FP4 and Int4 for post-quantization perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, and finetuning recovers 16-bit performance. Is the advantage mostly due to better codebook density near 0 for normal-like weights, or reduced saturation at outliers, or something about block-wise scaling synergy? Any ablations isolating what part of the NF4 design contributes most?

questions.title: Does double quantization introduce bias in dequantized scales, and does it matter?
questions.question_body: Double quantization centers $c_2$ by subtracting its mean before FP8 quantization. After dequantizing $c_2$, is there a noticeable bias or variance inflation in the recovered scales vs the original FP32? If so, does this bias systematically affect certain layers or block distributions, and how does the LoRA finetuning compensate for it?

questions.title: How does QLoRA’s inference memory footprint compute to 5 GB for LLaMA-7B?
questions.question_body: The paper states that the smallest Guanaco model (7B) requires about 5 GB at deployment. Can you break down this number into 4-bit base weights, quantization constants (with double quantization), LoRA adapter parameters (BF16 or FP16?), KV cache (for a given sequence length), and any additional buffers? I’d like to reproduce the 5 GB estimate.

questions.title: Why does finetuning on OASST1 (9k samples) beat much larger datasets like FLAN v2 subsamples?
questions.question_body: Results suggest data quality and task match matter more than sheer size for chatbot performance. What specific characteristics of OASST1 (e.g., multi-turn, diverse intents, human-authored, safety filters) do you think make it so effective relative to larger datasets? Any analyses that correlate dataset attributes to downstream Elo/Vicuna metrics?

questions.title: Why do MMLU and Vicuna/OA chatbot benchmark scores diverge so much?
questions.question_body: The paper finds strong MMLU performance does not imply strong chatbot performance and vice versa. Beyond obvious task mismatch, do you have evidence that certain finetuning distributions harm dialogic qualities (e.g., verbosity, helpfulness) even while improving factual QA? Are there feature-level diagnostics that predict when tuning for one benchmark will trade off against the other?

questions.title: How robust are GPT-4-based evaluations given the documented order bias?
questions.question_body: You report a significant ordering effect where GPT-4 rates the earlier response higher on average. Besides averaging over both orders, did you try prompt variants (e.g., chain-of-thought judge, blind scoring followed by reveal) to mitigate bias? Also, how large is the order effect numerically (e.g., average score delta), and does it differ across systems?

questions.title: How are ties handled in Elo computation for pairwise chatbot comparisons?
questions.question_body: The Elo setup allows ties. Which update rule do you use for a tie (e.g., outcome score 0.5 for both)? Do you use a standard $K=32$ across all comparisons and all systems, or tune $K$ per tournament? How sensitive are system rankings and confidence intervals to $K$, initial Elo, and random sampling order over 10,000 runs?

questions.title: Can you clarify the training schedule adjustments from 7B to 33B/65B in QLoRA?
questions.question_body: You mention that most hyperparameters found at 7B generalize, except learning rate (halved for 33B/65B) and batch size (doubled). What were the base settings (optimizer, weight decay, warmup, epochs), and what concrete values were used at each scale? Do larger models need fewer steps to converge under QLoRA because LoRA updates act as stronger regularizers?

questions.title: What explains QLoRA matching 16-bit LoRA and even full finetuning after 4-bit quantization?
questions.question_body: Prior work found 4-bit inference degrades quality, but QLoRA shows that 4-bit quantized bases with LoRA finetuning recover performance to match 16-bit LoRA and even full finetuning baselines. Is the intuition that LoRA layers adaptively correct quantization errors in activations and preactivations, making the precise base weights less critical after finetuning?

questions.title: Does NF4 assume all weight tensors are individually normal, and how true is that in practice?
questions.question_body: NF4’s optimality premise relies on weights being zero-centered normal with some $\sigma$. How closely do real pretrained LLM weight tensors match $N(0,1)$ after layer-wise rescaling? Are there layers (e.g., embeddings, layer norms, out projections) that deviate more (skewed, heavy tails), and does NF4 still outperform Int4/FP4 there?

questions.title: How does QLoRA handle outliers within a block despite using quantiles designed for normals?
questions.question_body: Block-wise quantization mitigates outlier impact vs global scaling, but within a 64-sized block there can still be outliers. Since NF4 codebook is fixed based on a normal distribution, how do extreme block values get represented without saturating? Does the use of per-block scaling via $c_2$ largely resolve this, or are there failure cases where saturation is common?

questions.title: What is the exact algorithm for selecting responses in multi-response datasets like OASST1?
questions.question_body: For datasets with multiple responses per prompt (like OASST1), the paper selects the top response at each conversation node. How is “top” determined—by human rating, upvotes, or some quality score? Does this introduce selection bias toward certain styles, and did you try training with all responses (e.g., sampled) to encourage diversity?

questions.title: How are gradients and memory for LoRA inputs computed and reduced via checkpointing?
questions.question_body: The paper states that with LoRA weights around 0.2% of base weights, LoRA input gradients can be 567 MB but reduced to 18 MB per sequence with gradient checkpointing. Could you detail how those numbers are computed (sequence length, hidden size, number of adapters), and how checkpointing reduces these gradients so dramatically?

questions.title: What happens if we reduce precision further (e.g., 3-bit base with LoRA)?
questions.question_body: The paper hints that since finetuning recovers information lost to 4-bit quantization, more aggressive quantization (e.g., 3-bit GPTQ for base weights) might still match 16-bit performance after LoRA finetuning. Are there preliminary results or theoretical expectations about where the break-even point lies in bits/parameter for QLoRA-like training?

questions.title: Does QLoRA dequantize weights per forward pass or cache dequantized tiles across steps?
questions.question_body: Since weights are frozen, could one dequantize once per step or per tile and reuse across microbatches to reduce overhead, or does memory pressure force on-the-fly dequantization every time? How does bitsandbytes implement this in its CUDA kernels for training vs inference scenarios?

questions.title: Are there known interactions between NF4 and activation quantization or KV cache quantization?
questions.question_body: QLoRA discusses weight quantization; however, inference often benefits from activation or KV cache quantization. Do NF4-quantized weights behave differently when combined with, say, 8-bit KV cache or 8-bit activations at inference? Any observed compounding errors or recommended practices when stacking these quantizations?
